teach: From the lesson: familia is the whole circle, the people who are yours — the word that holds every other family word inside it.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'La familia — the family. Familia is the whole circle, the people who are yours.' Another way to hold it: familia is the whole circle, the people who are yours — the word that holds every other family word inside it
walk: Walk it through: (1) Carmen opens the lesson with the biggest word of the day. (2) She defines la familia as the whole circle, the people who are yours. (3) That is: the family.

teach: From the lesson: padre is the formal word for father; papá is the warmer, everyday word, the one used at the kitchen table — dad.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Mi papá — my dad. Papá is the warmer, everyday word, the word a son uses at the kitchen table.' Another way to hold it: padre is the formal word for father; papá is the warmer, everyday word, the one used at the kitchen table — dad
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson gives two words for the same man: padre and papá. (2) Padre is the formal, respectful one. (3) Papá is the warm, everyday one — my dad.

teach: From the lesson: madre is mother, and like padre it carries respect in it; it is the partner word to mi padre.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Mi madre — my mother. Madre is mother, and like padre, it carries respect in it.' Another way to hold it: madre is mother, and like padre it carries respect in it; it is the partner word to mi padre
walk: Walk it through: (1) Mi means my. (2) Carmen defines madre right beside padre, as its partner word. (3) Madre is mother — so mi madre is my mother.

teach: From the lesson: hijos can mean sons, and it can also mean children together, sons and daughters in one word.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Mis hijos — my children. Hijos can mean sons, and it can also mean children together, sons and daughters in one word.' Another way to hold it: hijos can mean sons, and it can also mean children together, sons and daughters in one word
walk: Walk it through: (1) Mi hijo is one son and mi hija is one daughter. (2) For all the children together, the lesson uses the plural form. (3) That phrase is: Mis hijos.

q: Bill's sister Chelsea — which phrase names her in Spanish?
teach: From the lesson: hermana is sister, and Carmen names Chelsea with it directly: mi hermana Chelsea.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Mi hermana — my sister. Hermana is sister, and Chelsea is yours. Mi hermana.' Another way to hold it: hermana is sister, and Carmen names Chelsea with it directly: mi hermana Chelsea
walk: Walk it through: (1) Hermana means sister, and hermano means brother. (2) Chelsea is Bill's sister. (3) So she is named: Mi hermana Chelsea.

q: Carmen teaches that 'mi' means my for one person. What does 'mi' become in front of more than one person, as in 'my children'?
teach: From the lesson: Spanish shows the number right on the word: mi for one, mis for more than one — mi hijo, mis hijos.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Mi is for one thing, one person. Mis is for more than one. That is the entire rule, and it is a friendly rule, because English hides this — English says my for one child and my for five children and never blinks.' Another way to hold it: Spanish shows the number right on the word: mi for one, mis for more than one — mi hijo, mis hijos
walk: Walk it through: (1) In front of one person — padre, hermana, hijo — the word is mi. (2) In front of hijos, more than one, Carmen says it changes its coat. (3) The plural form is: mis.

q: What does the little word 'tu' mean, as in 'tu familia'?
teach: From the lesson: mi is my, for your own side of the table; tu is your, the friendly your used with family and friends.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Tu means your, the friendly your, the your you use with family and friends and people you are warm with.' Another way to hold it: mi is my, for your own side of the table; tu is your, the friendly your used with family and friends
walk: Walk it through: (1) Mi familia is my family — mi is my. (2) Carmen teaches the matching word for the other side of the table. (3) That word, tu, means: your.

q: Which phrase does Carmen teach for introducing someone — 'let me introduce you to Jillian'?
teach: From the lesson: te presento a… is the presentation ceremony: let me introduce you to — and it works for anyone you love.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Te presento a Jillian — I present to you Jillian, let me introduce you to Jillian.' Another way to hold it: te presento a… is the presentation ceremony: let me introduce you to — and it works for anyone you love
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson's ceremony has two parts: presenting the person, then saying who they are. (2) The presenting phrase is built on te presento a. (3) For Jillian, it is: Te presento a Jillian.

choices: let me introduce you to Jillian
q: What does 'Ella es mi prometida' mean?
teach: From the lesson: ella es means she is, and prometida is the fiancée — the promised one — so the sentence presents Jillian as Bill's fiancée.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Ella es mi prometida. Let me introduce you to Jillian. She is my fiancée.' Another way to hold it: ella es means she is, and prometida is the fiancée — the promised one — so the sentence presents Jillian as Bill's fiancée
walk: Walk it through: (1) Ella means she, and es means is. (2) Prometida, from lesson one, is the fiancée. (3) Joined: she is my fiancée.

q: Someone points at a photograph and wants to ask who the person is. What question does Carmen teach?
teach: From the lesson: quién means who, and es means is — the question for asking about a person in a photograph or across a room.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: '¿Quién es? — who is he, who is she, who is that? Quién means who. ¿Quién es? Say it with me, with the curiosity in it: ¿Quién es? Someone shows you a family photograph — a beautiful old picture, a man you do not know standing tall — and you ask: ¿Quién es? And the answer comes back in exactly the shapes you now own: Es mi padre — he is my father.' Another way to hold it: quién means who, and es means is — the question for asking about a person in a photograph or across a room
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson teaches the mirror of presenting: asking who someone is. (2) Quién means who. (3) The question is: ¿Quién es?

q: Carmen previews two words for after the wedding on March the twenty-fifth. After that day, what will Jillian be in Spanish — Bill's what?
teach: From the lesson: today Jillian is mi prometida, the fiancée; after the wedding, Spanish gives her a new title — esposa, wife.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Esposa — wife. La esposa — the wife. Mi esposa — my wife. Say it with me, just to taste the future: Mi esposa.' Another way to hold it: today Jillian is mi prometida, the fiancée; after the wedding, Spanish gives her a new title — esposa, wife
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson previews the future pair: esposo, husband, and esposa, wife. (2) Jillian is the woman, so her word takes the -a form. (3) After the wedding she is: mi esposa.

q: In your own words: what is the difference between 'mi' and 'mis', and when do you use each one?
teach: From the lesson: one machine, two settings: the word for my changes to show whether one person or more than one stands after it.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Mi is for one thing, one person. Mis is for more than one. That is the entire rule, and it is a friendly rule, because English hides this — English says my for one child and my for five children and never blinks.' Another way to hold it: one machine, two settings: the word for my changes to show whether one person or more than one stands after it
walk: Walk it through: (1) Both words mean my. (2) In front of one person — mi padre, mi hijo — Carmen uses mi. (3) In front of more than one — mis hijos — the word becomes mis.
